lede: The current official run has {nTasks} tasks in {nCats} categories: an AI coding agent works alone on each for {minMin}–{maxMin} minutes and is stopped the moment time is up.

defs: A timed benchmark for AI coding agents. The tasks run from Lean formal proofs, olympiad mathematics, extremal constructions, performance optimization and Luban lock disassembly all the way to designing and building complete web works and a desktop system.
Each model is tested together with its own agent harness, such as Claude Code or Codex, at reasoning effort `xhigh` by default.
Every task starts in a fresh session and is worked on alone, with nobody answering questions; reminders, resuming and isolation are under [How Tests Run](#format).

Standard tasks deliver proofs, constructions, source code or disassembly routes and are scored by programs that check the answers; design tasks deliver web works or desktop projects that run as they are, graded once each by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT 6.1 Sol and averaged.
Each task is converted to a 0–100 score, and the weighted sum is the model's total; see [Scoring](#scoring).

overview: The 6 tasks in Math Reasoning, Algorithm Contests and Spatial Reasoning are standard tasks; the 6 in the other 5 categories are design tasks. Click a task name to open its page.

All five web tasks must run completely in Chrome by double-clicking `index.html`, with no web server; Nested Operating Systems uses Electron 45.2.1 or another host that can embed Chromium, launched from a single entry point.
Weights go to categories first and are split evenly among the tasks inside each category (5% each for the three Algorithm Contests tasks).

tasks.lead: Scoring rules for standard tasks are drawn in each category's figure; design tasks keep their scoring directions and points in a fold.

formal-proof.scoring: 8 problems, 0 or 12.5 points each, 100 in all
points: **Formalization**: break a paper proof into a chain of lemmas Lean accepts, finding the matching definitions, theorems and names in Mathlib.
**Zero tolerance**: the Lean kernel checks every step; one `sorry` or one compile error and the problem scores nothing.
**Choosing and focusing**: the eight problems differ in field and difficulty; take the sure ones first and finish one before starting the next.

math-olympiad.scoring: 0–7 per problem, 126 in all, scaled to 100
points: **Original, so nothing to look up**: the problems are new and unpublished, with no known solutions to recall.
**Find, then prove**: after the answer, argue both directions: it is attained, and nothing does better or no other solution exists.
**Rigorous write-up**: every key step written out to olympiad grading standards, without spelling out the rest endlessly.
**One problem at a time**: write each solution into its file as soon as it is done; if a problem resists, write down the progress and move on.

unit-square.scoring: Ratio to the reference construction, looked up on an anchor table
points: **Search strategy**: maximizing a minimum is not smooth and has many local optima; standard methods soon hit a plateau.
**Exactness**: if rounding puts even one point outside, the whole answer is invalid, so results must be rechecked from the written values.
**Using the compute**: organize a parallel search across the 14 logical processors and one GPU.
**Knowing when to turn**: when one direction stalls, judge when to switch ideas.

transformer.scoring: The 8 public shapes each scored by speedup on an anchor table, then averaged
points: **Matrix work on the GPU**: matrix multiplication, softmax and layer normalization are all hand-written; kernel throughput sets the ceiling.
**Precision and tolerance**: internal precision is free to choose, but results must stay within tolerance.

**Memory and platform limits**: very long sequences cannot hold an $S\times S$ intermediate, and work must be split into batches; running it all at once can reset the driver or even crash the machine.
**Tuning per shape**: the 8 shapes range from ten thousand short sequences to a single sequence of 100,000 tokens, and tiling, layout and precision can be chosen per shape.

circuit.scoring: The 24 public circuits each scored by speedup on an anchor table, averaged, then times a correctness factor
points: **Bit-level parallelism**: pack many independent stimuli into 64-bit words and AVX2 vectors and compute them together.
**Circuit preprocessing**: gates are not given in dependency order; sorting, simplification and layout decide how fast evaluation is.
**Threads and caches**: with many stimuli and large circuits, batching, layout and division of work set the ceiling.
**Tuning per class**: the 8 classes, from deep chains and wide grids to multipliers, cipher rounds and register files, differ in topology, and strategy can be chosen per class.

luban.scoring: 8 puzzles in three tiers, each scoring $w \times \min(1, B/N)$ by step count, 100 in all
points: **Spatial imagination**: work out every piece's shape, position and interlocks from the layer drawings and voxel data.
**Reasoning about blocking**: judge by hand whether each move collides; one collision voids the whole route.
**Full disassembly**: after splitting into two groups, keep going until every group is a single piece.
**Fewer steps**: among legal routes, find shorter ones with fewer changes of group, axis and direction.
**Coupling**: dozens of features pull on one another, and any change must flow down the dependency chain in real time.
**Procedural geometry**: output from paths, text, operators and node groups feeds on into solids, deformation, emission and collision.
**3D and particles**: real extrusion, holes, bevels and deformation with materials, shadows and depth of field; deformed geometry drives particles, collision events and trails.
**The 15-second piece**: an opening, development, build-up and close, with the main elements carried through rather than a reel of unrelated feature clips.
**3D art**: finely modelled scenes, towers, enemies and bosses with distinct silhouettes, and continuous moving, attacking and hit reactions.
**Dynamic pathfinding**: isolation, destruction, bypass and boss terrain changes all recompute every path, and the way may never be sealed off.
**Mechanics carry the theme**: route length, fire coverage, tower survival and spending trade off, and each map calls for its own defence.
**Readable information**: with many enemies and effects on screen, routes, node states and health stay clear.
directions: Tower and enemy models and animation
Telling towers, enemies and map apart

points: **Soft-body deformation**: local denting, overall bulging and staggered rebound, with the jelly's reaction changing the heavy ball's motion.
**Fluid and buoyancy**: density decides where balls settle, and waves set the surface, the water and the bottom moving differently at once.
**Three-way coupling**: soft bodies, rigid bodies and fluid act on one another, with deformation and waves clearly layered.
**Choosing and joining libraries**: whether and where to use a physics library is the model's call, and the parts must add up to one believable motion.
**Continuous transitions**: the same B200 changes form between package, floor plan, data and system, and transitions can stop and run backwards.
**Multi-scale modelling**: from solder balls, microbumps and TSVs up to racks, every scale holds up close.
**SVG motion graphics**: bit fields, number lines, multiply-accumulate and link topologies deform themselves and stay aligned with the 3D.
**Linked state**: precision, inputs and selections persist across chapters and map to the same part, data or device.
**Grasp of style**: toon rendering must balance the finish of a model with the simplification of anime backgrounds, with sunshine and rain holding at once.
**Modelling workload**: dozens of objects that stay recognizable and detailed up close.
**Light and colour**: high-key, low-contrast sunshower light, a cyan-white palette with a few warm gold highlights.
**Choreographed motion**: changes travel along the path of wind, cloud and waves, restrained in size and staggered in rhythm.
directions: Quay wall, underwater and breakwater blocks
Embankment, mooring and signs of life

points: **The kernel is a program**: scheduling, messages, files and window management really run as programs inside the system, not as calls back to the host.
**Competition and isolation**: under a shared multi-level budget every process keeps getting time, and a runaway program only hurts its own quota.
**State and causality**: after snapshots, restores and forks, processes, messages, files and images still match the same moment.
**Closed-loop flight**: the flight is decided by the flight-control program, scheduling budget and inputs together, and recordings can be replayed and branched.

blocks: While the session is running, a reminder is inserted at the model's next tool call (through a hook in Claude Code, through `turn/steer` in Codex); when the session is idle, the host starts a new round with it.

ul: Each reminder is sent once per stretch; the overall-progress hint counts total time on the task, so a resumed session does not get it again.
An overall-progress hint missed during an interruption is sent when work resumes; if the resumed stretch starts with 10 minutes or less, it is skipped and the submit reminder is sent at once.
When several timed reminders pile up, only the latest is delivered.

head: Situation
Handling
rows: API error, quota exhausted, host crash
Close the session; time left = this stretch's limit − time used, rounded up to the minute; reconnect to the original session with that time, never restarting from scratch
Says the session was interrupted by a system failure, that progress is kept, and restates the opening rules, without giving the time left
The original session cannot be reconnected
Open a new session in the same work folder and mention the system failure and the latest commit
A third failure on the same task
No more extra time; recorded as “anomaly (time already extended)”
Failures after time is up, or a forced fallback stop
Another batch has the machine to itself
Wait until that batch is out of time and cleaned up, then resume, without breaking its exclusive use
Investigate and launch once more; a second failure is recorded as a launch failure

ul: **Account**: the tested account is an ordinary one outside the administrators group; agents run with `bypassPermissions` (Claude Code) or `approvalPolicy=never` (Codex).
**Logs**: session logs are moved where the tested account cannot read them once the session closes.
**Browser MCP**: chrome-devtools-mcp, with a fresh temporary user-data folder each time.

**Machine**: answering and grading happen on the same machine: Windows 11, Intel Core i7-14700KF (8 performance cores + 12 efficiency cores, 28 logical processors), NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 (16 GB), 64 GB of memory.

format.title: The Two Test Batches

head: Batch
How
Why
rows: 10 tasks at once; the unit square task is pinned to 14 logical processors (8 threads of 4 performance cores + 6 efficiency cores)

None needs the machine to itself while answering. AE, tower defense, physics, nested OS and the two visual tasks are not scored on smoothness or frame rate; the unit square task uses all its compute for search, and every model gets the same processors
Transformer and circuit simulation one after the other, each with the whole machine
Answering means timing over and over, and other load would disturb the timings

blocks: Once a whole batch is out of time, leftover processes of the tested account are ended (keeping each session's host) before the next batch starts; during the serial batch, nothing that loads the CPU or GPU runs.

scoringLead: Each task's scoring directions and points are under [Tasks and What They Test](#tasks); this section covers the mechanics only.

ul: $S_t$ is task $t$'s score scaled to 0–100, and $w_t$ is its weight.
A category's score is the weighted average of its tasks.
A failed grading pass is retried at most once; a task still missing a required pass is not scaled up from the remaining items, counts as 0 in the total for now and is marked provisional.
Items, task scores and totals keep one decimal place; weights are exact and never rounded.

details.title: Extremal construction: anchor table
blocks: Maximizing the smallest triangle in a unit square: $r=\Delta/\Delta^*$, where $\Delta^*$ is the fixed reference construction for $n=30$ (the best known value as of September 2026):

ul: The baseline is a general optimized solution written by the task setter, its code not public; it and the submission run interleaved in the same evaluation, 3 times each, taking the median.
Both run under the same conditions: the same set of 16 logical processors, high priority and the same environment variables; only the wall-clock time of the single call to the core function counts.
$R_i$ and $C_i$ are the baseline's and the submission's times on input $i$, $s_i=R_i/C_i$; $k$ is the number of correctness inputs the circuit task passes.

scoring.title: Scoring Design Tasks
blocks: The guide gives each task 4–8 directions and 19–37 items, listing only the points and a one-line scoring note; graders score directly within the points, full marks meaning that point is done excellently, and decimals are allowed.

principles.title: Setting
items: **More work than time on purpose**: design tasks hold more than can be finished in the time. What counts is what gets done first, how complete it is and how good.

**Statements say what, not how**: a statement gives the theme, content and requirements; algorithms, libraries and code structure are left to the model. A clearly better technique is written as a requirement, and pitfalls of the running environment are stated plainly.

**Written for how strong models read**: only design intent and the concrete content of the work. Values that can be inferred, results that follow naturally when the system is right, and words describing feelings are left out; low-point features get a sentence or two.

**Difficulty is calibrated by real runs**: AI estimates of time and difficulty are not trusted; to judge difficulty, a model actually does the task. The olympiad problems were picked from original candidates by measured solving time, then ordered by difficulty using the official scores and blind solving times.

principles.title: Answering
items: **Plain statements, no pressure**: statements and injected prompts are plain instructions, never phrases like “capability contest” or “compared with other models”. Zero-score and deduction rules live only in the grading guides; statements only tell the model that grading is lenient about submission format.

**The two kinds are treated differently**: design tasks are asked to push completeness against the statement, and the odd small bug barely affects the score; standard tasks are only asked to solve as the statement says.
**Use all the time**: committed versions are a safety net, so big changes are safe; a round that ends early with time to spare is picked up by [immediate continuation](#format-3).

principles.title: Grading
items: **Grading follows the statement**: grading guides list directions and items according to the statement's scoring criteria. Design-task directions are independent, and each thing counts in one item only.

**What can be computed goes to tools**: Lean compilation, the extremal objective, performance speedups, and the legality and step count of Luban lock routes are all computed exactly by tools. Graders only judge what needs judging.

**Discrimination where strong models are**: extremal construction and performance tasks interpolate on anchor tables whose slope grows from the low range to the upper-middle range. Standard methods only reach the low range; works at an upper-middle level pull clearly ahead.

end: The original statements, grading guides and evaluation scripts are in the [GitHub repository](gh:). Each task's statement is linked from its task page.

designscore.cellNote: One cell per point, so cells show the points; the filled part is the score awarded
